sections.title: What is being reversed?
sections.label: Inverse process

blocks.html: Integration reverses differentiation by finding functions with the specified derivative.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Check the antiderivative by differentiating back to the integrand.

blocks.title: Recover a particular curve from its gradient
blocks.prompt:
A curve has gradient function \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=18 x^{2} - 2\).

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.
blocks.hint: An antiderivative gives a family. Use the point only after writing the family.
blocks.solution:
Find a function whose derivative is the stated gradient. Add the unknown constant.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(18 x^{2} - 2\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(C + 6 x^{3} - 2 x\).

retry.feedback: Substitute the given coordinates after integrating. They determine C.

blocks.html: A derivative alone does not determine the constant value.

blocks.title: Recover a particular curve from its gradient

blocks.solution:
Write the curve as \(y=C + 6 x^{3} - 5 x\). Substituting the coordinates gives \(-3=-1+C\).

Answer: \(-2\).

retry.feedback: Substitute the given coordinates after integrating. They determine C.

What is being reversed?

Integration reverses differentiation by finding functions with the specified derivative.

Why is there an arbitrary constant?

Adding any constant makes a vertical translation whose derivative is unchanged.

How does a point select one curve?

  1. \(C + 7 x^{3}\)
  2. \(C + 7 x^{3} - 2 x\)
  3. \(C + 7 x^{3} - x\)
  4. \(7 x^{3} - x\)

Find a function whose derivative is the stated gradient. Add the unknown constant.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(21 x^{2} - 1\). Every constant has derivative zero.

sections.title: What happens to an exponent when integrating?
sections.label: Raise power

blocks.html: For \(n\ne-1\), add one to the exponent n and then divide by the new exponent.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Integrate term by term. Add a single arbitrary constant at the end.

blocks.title: Integrate powers and use a point to fix the constant
blocks.prompt:
The integrand is \(4 x^{2} - x - 1\).

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.
blocks.hint: Add one to each exponent, divide by the new exponent and handle an exponent of −1 separately.
blocks.solution:
Integrate each power after simplifying.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(4 x^{2} - x - 1\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(C + \frac{4 x^{3}}{3} - \frac{x^{2}}{2} - x\).

retry.feedback: The integral of a constant is a linear term. The arbitrary constant is in addition to that term.

blocks.html: Dividing by the old exponent does not reverse the power rule.

blocks.title: Integrate powers and use a point to fix the constant
blocks.prompt:
The integrand is \(8 x^{4} - 5 x + 9\).

For a particular antiderivative, the value at \(x=3\) is \(\frac{4023}{10}\). Find the constant in the form shown by your antiderivative.
blocks.hint: Add one to each exponent, divide by the new exponent and handle an exponent of −1 separately.
blocks.solution:
Use the particular form \(F(x)=\frac{8 x^{5}}{5} - \frac{5 x^{2}}{2} + 9 x+C\). Its non-constant part has value \(\frac{3933}{10}\) at this input.

Answer: \(C=9\).

retry.feedback: The integral of a constant is a linear term. The arbitrary constant is in addition to that term.

blocks.title: Integrate a trigonometric function in radians
blocks.prompt:
The integrand is \(11 \sin{\left(2 x + \frac{\pi}{5} \right)} - 2\). Angles are in radians.

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.
blocks.hint: Use standard sine, cosine or secant-squared antiderivatives and divide by the inner slope.
blocks.solution:
The antiderivative of sine is negative cosine. Then divide by the inner derivative.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(11 \sin{\left(2 x + \frac{\pi}{5} \right)} - 2\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(C - 2 x - \frac{11 \cos{\left(2 x + \frac{\pi}{5} \right)}}{2}\).

blocks.title: Integrate a trigonometric function in radians
blocks.prompt:

Subtract its value at \(- \frac{\pi}{15}\) from its value at \(\frac{\pi}{10}\).

revision.body:
Which antiderivative gives sine?

The derivative of \(-\cos x\) is \(\sin x\).

Which antiderivative gives cosine?

Sine differentiates to cosine in radian measure.

How does tangent appear when integrating?

Tangent differentiates to secant squared when the angle is measured in radians.

Quick worked example

The integrand is \(- 9 \cos{\left(8 x + \frac{5 \pi}{14} \right)} - 4\). Angles are in radians.

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.

  1. \(C - 3 x - \frac{9 \sin{\left(8 x + \frac{5 \pi}{14} \right)}}{8}\)
  2. \(C - 5 x - \frac{9 \sin{\left(8 x + \frac{5 \pi}{14} \right)}}{8}\)
  3. \(C - 4 x - \frac{9 \sin{\left(8 x + \frac{5 \pi}{14} \right)}}{8}\)
  4. \(- 4 x - \frac{9 \sin{\left(8 x + \frac{5 \pi}{14} \right)}}{8}\)

The antiderivative of sine is negative cosine. Then divide by the inner derivative.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(- 9 \cos{\left(8 x + \frac{5 \pi}{14} \right)} - 4\). Every constant has derivative zero.

• Cosine without the negative sign differentiates to negative sine.
  • A constant term integrates to a multiple of x.

sections.title: Why does one over x need a different rule?
sections.label: Exception

blocks.html: For \(x>0\), differentiating \(\ln x\) gives \(\frac1x\).

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Use a natural logarithm instead of the integration power rule at exponent −1.

blocks.title: Integrate a reciprocal and stay on one side of its pole
blocks.prompt:
The integrand is \(\frac{11}{x}\). Work on \(x>0\).

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.
blocks.hint: Confirm the denominator never reaches zero between the limits.
blocks.solution:
The integral power rule excludes exponent −1. Use a logarithm and keep the reciprocal of the linear gradient.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(\frac{11}{x}\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(11\ln\left|x\right|+C\).

retry.feedback: The ordinary integration power rule fails when the new exponent would be zero. A logarithm handles that case.

blocks.html: Adding one to −1 would give a zero denominator in the power rule.

blocks.title: Integrate a reciprocal and stay on one side of its pole
blocks.prompt:
The integrand is \(\frac{6}{x}\). Work on \(x>0\).

blocks.hint: Confirm the denominator never reaches zero between the limits.
blocks.solution:
The variable part of an antiderivative is \(6 \ln{\left(x \right)}\).

Subtract its value at \(2\) from its value at \(16\).

Answer: \(\ln{\left(262144 \right)}\).

revision.body:
Why does one over x need a different rule?

For \(x>0\), differentiating \(\ln x\) gives \(\frac1x\).

What factor goes before the logarithm?

The derivative of the denominator is part of the chain rule for a logarithm.

Why must both limits stay on the same side of a pole?

A reciprocal is not continuous where its denominator is zero.

Quick worked example

The integrand is \(\frac{8}{x}\). Work on \(x>0\).

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.

  1. \(C + x + 8 \ln{\left(x \right)}\)
  2. \(C - x + 8 \ln{\left(x \right)}\)
  3. \(8\ln\left|x\right|+C\)
  4. \(8 \ln{\left(x \right)}\)

The integral power rule excludes exponent −1. Use a logarithm and keep the reciprocal of the linear gradient.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(\frac{8}{x}\). Every constant has derivative zero.
revision.checks:
• Adding one to −1 would give a zero denominator in the power rule.
  • A logarithmic antiderivative of a reciprocal has a factor from the denominator.

revision.body:
Which endpoint is subtracted?

The definite integral over a continuous interval is the antiderivative at the upper limit minus its value at the lower limit.

What happens when limits are reversed?

Exchanging the bounds changes the sign of the integral.

What if the function contains a reciprocal?

The ordinary evaluation uses an antiderivative on an interval where the integrand is continuous.

Quick worked example

The integrand is \(5 x^{3} - 7 x - 6\) on the interval whose endpoints are \(-1\) and \(1\).

Evaluate \(\int_{-1}^{1}5 x^{3} - 7 x - 6\,\mathrm dx\) exactly.

The variable part of an antiderivative is \(\frac{5 x^{4}}{4} - \frac{7 x^{2}}{2} - 6 x\).

Subtract its value at \(-1\) from its value at \(1\).
revision.checks:
• Do not ignore the lower substitution even if the lower bound is zero.
  • The mathematically upper written limit can be numerically smaller than the lower written limit.
revision.examTip: Write both endpoint evaluations before rounding or simplifying.

revision.body:
When does the definite integral equal an area?

On an interval where the curve is above or on the x-axis, its integral is the area beneath it.

Why can the definite integral be negative?

The integral counts a region below the axis with a negative sign. Its geometric area is positive.

How do you add areas across an axis crossing?

A crossing divides the region into pieces with different signs.

Quick worked example

A curve has equation \(y=\left(3 - x\right) \left(10 x + 20\right)\).

Find the x-values where the curve meets the x-axis.

Set \(\left(3 - x\right) \left(10 x + 20\right)\) equal to zero and use the two linear factors.

Answer: \(-2, 3\).
revision.checks:
• A graph with an x-intercept can still lie entirely above the axis on the requested interval.
  • State the area as a positive value.
revision.examTip: Sketch the crossings and label your split points before integrating.
